questions.question: British codebreaking machine used during World War II.
questions.explanation: Colossus was used at Bletchley Park to decrypt German messages.

questions.question: Alan Turing's theoretical computing machine concept.
questions.explanation: The Turing Machine is a theoretical model of computation.

questions.question: First Apple computer with a graphical user interface.
questions.explanation: The Apple Lisa (1983) was Apple's first computer with a GUI; the Macintosh (1984) popularized it a year later.

questions.question: Research facility where the transistor was invented.
questions.explanation: Bell Labs invented the transistor in 1947.

questions.question: Computer that defeated chess world champion Garry Kasparov.
questions.explanation: IBM's Deep Blue defeated Kasparov in 1997.

questions.question: First integrated circuit component used in third generation computers.
questions.explanation: ICs combined multiple transistors on a single chip.

questions.question: Computer language developed for teaching programming.
questions.explanation: BASIC was designed for beginners in the 1960s.

questions.question: First portable computer released in 1981.
questions.explanation: The Osborne 1 was the first commercially successful portable computer.

questions.question: Protocol suite that became the foundation of the Internet.
questions.explanation: TCP/IP was developed in the 1970s for ARPANET.

questions.question: Company that created the first smartphone.
questions.explanation: IBM's Simon was the first smartphone, released in 1994.

questions.question: Engineer called the 'father of supercomputing' who designed the CDC 6600 and Cray-1.
questions.explanation: Seymour Cray designed record-setting machines at CDC and later founded Cray Research.

questions.question: Onboard computer that guided Apollo 11 to the Moon in 1969.
questions.explanation: The AGC pioneered integrated circuits and ran the landing with just 4 KB of RAM.

questions.question: First self-replicating program, an early virus unleashed on ARPANET in 1971.
questions.explanation: Creeper spread between PDP-10 machines displaying 'I'M THE CREEPER: CATCH ME IF YOU CAN'; Reaper was written to delete it.

questions.question: Approximate number of vacuum tubes inside ENIAC.
questions.explanation: ENIAC used roughly 17,500-18,000 tubes, causing frequent failures across its 30-ton frame.

questions.question: Mathematician known as the 'father of information theory'.
questions.explanation: Shannon's 1948 paper founded information theory, defining the bit and channel capacity.

questions.question: ENIAC filled a room and used about 18,000 vacuum tubes. Which 1947 invention made computers dramatically smaller and more reliable?
questions.explanation: The transistor replaced bulky, heat-prone vacuum tubes and launched second-generation computers.

questions.question: A museum labels machines by generation: vacuum tubes first, transistors second, integrated circuits third. A 1981 PC built around a single-chip CPU belongs to which generation?
questions.explanation: Fourth-generation computers are defined by the microprocessor, which put an entire CPU on one chip.

questions.question: In 1969 engineers linked computers at UCLA, Stanford, UC Santa Barbara, and Utah into a four-node network. Name this direct ancestor of the Internet.
questions.explanation: ARPANET pioneered packet switching between those four sites and evolved into today's Internet.

questions.question: Which 1957 programming language, still used for scientific and engineering computation, was the first widely implemented high-level language?
questions.explanation: Fortran (FORmula TRANslation) proved high-level languages could rival hand-written assembly for speed.

questions.question: In 1991 a Finnish student released a free hobby operating-system kernel that now powers most servers, supercomputers, and Android phones. Name it.
questions.explanation: Linus Torvalds posted the Linux kernel in 1991; combined with GNU tools it became the dominant server OS.
